I have two friends in the Internet Security business, and both of them
have told me that if the options are to allow full access to the internet
to all employees (with security on company PCs, obviously) or to allow
limited access to the internet to all employees, they ALWAYS choose
to be more restrictive (e.g. "This site is unavailable...") rather than
less.

When asked why, they both said the same thing: There will always be
users that try to download what they aren't supposed to download, so
better safe than sorry.

That being the case, I'd suggest that the groups in-question aren't doing
it correctly. Here is a better strategy, with less misery for everyone.

If they are using decklists since they KNOW that certain players are/have
cheated, they should have ejected those cheaters, reported them to the
VEKN, told them not to come back for a year (or whatever), and then
they wouldn't have had to use decklists.

If they are using decklists since they THINK that certain players are/have
cheated, they should be taken aside and have it explained to them that
certain actions look like cheating and that, without making any judgements,
it must be stated that cheating isn't allowed, and these kinds of things
will be CLOSELY WATCHED. Hopefully that would remove the incentive
for those cheaters to cheat in that playgroup. If not, then see above.

Cheaters should be punished and ostracized, not tolerated via decklists.

Not generally, if the judge has reason to believe the circumstances
warrant different handling.

For example, if a table was being set up and it collapsed and the
players reassembled their decks in a hurry and, as I walked by, I found
a copy of Wake With Evening's Freshness nestling next to someone's bag,
I'd likely treat that pretty differently to finding a copy of Malkavian
Dementia in a deck that suddenly finds itself in a final with three
Malkavian decks.

As the judging guidelines say:

"If the judge believes that the situation has significant,
extenuating circumstances, he or she is free to modify the penalty
as appropriate."

Which is to say, I'd generally go along with a harsh penalty - Game Loss
generally, rather than instant Disqualification - but judges are
empowered and encouraged to bear the whole situation in mind.
(Obviously, at the final, GL and DQ are the same thing.) And note that
the default penalties generally assume unintentional infractions - you
can upgrade for players who are obviously being cocks.

There's also the long-standing question of how / where deck list
checking should be handled, relative to the final. Some players have in
the past suggested that the checks on the finalists' decks should be
handled at the end of the previous round. If your deck is illegal, you
lose the game you've just finished (0GW, 0VP - possibly even 0TP), but
could requalify for the final if your earlier scores are still strong
enough. So if I got 3 GWs and 11VP, I could still potentially get into
the final with 2GWs and 7VP, when my 4VP third game is knocked out.

Alternatively, you could knock out their strongest game - so if I got
5VP in the first round and 2VP in the second round (2R+F), my deck list
infraction as a finalist would knock out round one and leave me with
round two only.

Certainly, I wouldn't try to impose this sort of thing on a tournament
*now* (because it's not possible under the current rules), but it might
be a viable option for the future.

Alternatively again, you could hand a player their decklist in ten
minutes before the final, ask *them* to check it, and then do the judge
check afterwards. This should remove the unintentional "Whoops, I have
LSJ's copy of Gather in my Toreador deck" sort of slip-ups.

--

Sure. But if you are using decklists 'cause people in the past have
cheated in ways that using decklists would fix? Kevin's post is
completely reasonable--rather than blanket punishing *everyone* (i.e.
requiring deck lists and DQing people for what are likely just honest
mistakes), just specifically punish the people cheating. If you catch
someone actually cheating? Sure. DQ them. You can do that *without* a
blanket deck list policy.

> The organizers might just use decklist since the think that some
> (random, unknown) players will cheat. It does happen, even if you have
> a speech before the tournament.

Sure. But again, deck lists don't stop people from cheating. People
will cheat if they want to cheat. If they think they can't get away
with cheating due to deck lists, they'll cheat in some other way. I
suspect that VTES players break down into 2 groups:

-People who aren't going to cheat (the vast majority)

-People who will cheat (the vast minority)

And if you are willing to cheat, you are willing to cheat. If you
can't cheat by changing your deck, you'll cheat by not spending enough
pool or by "forgetting" a DNR clause or by looking at someone's hand
or whatever. So you can make a blanket rule (deck lists and DQs for
irregular decks) that might stop one form of cheating, but also will
punish completely innocent players (the vast majority of the players)
for being sloppy, tired, or hung over. Or, conversely, you can *not*
make a blanket punishment rule, and just be a judge and use your
judgement. And if someone seems to be cheating, call them out on it
and do what you need to do.

> And the use of decklists doesn't mean that judges won't CLOSELY WATCH
> for other forms of cheating. It just means that changing your deck is
> one form of cheating that will be quite hard to get away with.

Maybe, maybe not. How are the deck lists used? If there are deck
lists, when are the checked? Randomly? That being the case, if the
advantages of cheating outweigh the likelyhood of getting checked,
cheaters will still cheat. Before the final? Then you illegally modify
your deck during the prelims and put it back to original form before
the final. Do you check every deck at the start of the tournament?
Then you change it after it has been checked. If people want to cheat,
they are going to cheat. But I suspect that the vast majority of
players aren't going to cheat in the first place.

> I don't see how you tolerate cheaters by the use of decklists. Sure,
> if all you do is tell people to hand in a decklist and then you don't
> care about anything else. But that's not how it usually goes.

Well, no. His point was (as I understand it) that deck lists are a
knee jerk blanket reaction to people cheating. If last time, someone
cheated by changing their deck, and your reaction is "next time I'll
use deck lists...", that is less effective than "This time, I'll DQ
that guy".

-Peter

> By that reasoning there'd be no point in rules against cheating at
> all?

No, that isn't the case at all. But if people are getting DQed for
minor deck list infractions that are likely the result of honest
mistake, then the system has failed. And should be changed.

> Removing one possible way of cheating has to be better than
> removing none of the possible ways? And, as I said, there's nothing in
> using decklists that prohibits organizers from dealing with other
> types of cheating as well.

Sure. But as deck lists tend to have ironclad, blanket penalties
atteched to them, they tend to result in undesirable results. If
people want to use deck lists, go nuts. But people should not be
getting DQ'ed for minor deck inconsistiencies that are far more likely
the result of honest mistake than cheating.

> You can use decklist and use judgement at the same time?

Sure. But to this point, all reports of people being DQed due to deck
list irregularity seem to fall on the side of "We just drew the hard
line!" than "Well, judgement indicated that he was cheating rather
than it was an honest mistake." If you want to use deck lists, go
crazy. But again, people should not be getting DQed 'cause their deck
is off a couple cards for what is likely an honest error. If someone
has the same problem 3 tournaments in a row? Yeah, probably cheating.
If their deck is wildly different than the deck list should indicate?
If someone who has never show any indication of cheating has 2 or 3
missing cards in their deck? Probably not cheating.

> I don't understand the horror in writing down your deck (something
> lots of people do anyway, to post on the newsgroup etc) and handing
> the paper over to the organizer.

There is no horror. Unless you get DQed due to a deck list check, and
your deck is missing a couple cards (that accidentally got left in
your deck box) or picked up a couple extra cards (from the deck it was
next to).

> How the decklists are used is up to the organizers, ofc. And that can
> be discussed, since there are surely better and worse ways to use
> them. It's not a bulletproof system though, I agree.

Sure. But if people are getting DQed for what are in all likelyhood
perfectly innocent errors, they are being used badly.

> How about if the reaction is "This time, I'll DQ that guy" AND "next
> time I'll use decklists"?
> Using decklists in your following tournaments doesn't make you unable
> to DQ people in your current one.

No, it doesn't. But if you can DQ people for cheating without using
deck lists, why bother in the first place? Again, I have never been to
a tournament that used deck lists in my life. Ever. I have never run a
tournament that used deck lists. I have never felt the need or that
anyone was cheating 'cause they weren't in use. I mean, yeah, ok, if
you feel they are necessary, then use them. More power to you. But I'm
unconvinced that they are necessary or even particularly helpful in
the long run. But that is me.

-Peter

mistype (e.g. writing only Sudden), a confounded entry (e.g. Ingrid Russo
vs. Ingrid Rossler, Victoria vs. Victoria Ash), or a potential
loss/addition during the games (e.g. missing 1 Disarm and having 89
cards).
In these cases I've never seen any penalty; the decision was always to
correct the deck or decklist in the obvious way.

If the discrepancy is functional (there are actually different cards
written on the decklist and included in the deck) then the penalty is
usually Game Loss. I've not yet seen (or admistered) an actual DQ for
this (although due to how Archon handles the finalists, technically a
DQ is administered to remove them from the finals). I wasn't present at
this game in question, so I'm not sure whether an actual DQ was issued
or whether it is just a GL that was technically issed as a DQ. But on

> methods...", it could hardly be called futile.

I don't really see that going anywhere.

Sure it's not mandatory to issue anything. Nor are requesting decklists
mandatory to begin with. I think it's good to have the kind of
discussion where we discuss whether it makes sense to have decklists at
all for tournaments. Or, for that matter, whether changing the contents
of the decks between rounds should be prohibited at all. But I digress.
Let's assume for now that the contents of the decks are not allowed to
be changed between rounds, and a decklist is requested.

If everybody knows that the practice is to issue a Game Loss in any case
there is a non-typo, non-mistype, non-ingame lost/"gained" difference
between the decklist and the deck, everybody is fully motivated to:
1) make sure they jot down the contents of their decks accurately, and
2) not change anything on the deck between rounds (especially important
and trackable for the finals, where due to scouting there is the
highest likelihood that game-specific information can be beneficial
to the player).

If everybody knows that the practice is to issue a Warning (or lower
penalty) in such cases, there is effectively no penalty. As you need
multiple transgressions of the same type during the same tournament
for the penalties to escalate, issuing a Warning for this is equal
to issuing no penalty at all.

If there is a limit (written or practiced) of, say, X cards, to what
difference is tolerable before the penalty of Game Loss is
administered, then that basically means: change X cards as you see
fit. If we want to encourage changing the contents of the decks,
then sure, doing this is recommended. Otherwise, it is not. Plus,
there is the question whether you force the player to switch back
to the decklist or alter the decklist to mirror the deck (giving
players different options to change their decks).

As for fairness... On one hand the player who made an honest
mistake by, say, for whatever reason not being able to count all
his 102 cards and write them down properly (let's say he was
traveling for a long time, and had no time to write the decklist
before the event, and was pretty tired and made a couple of
mistakes, or managed to trade in a Heart of Cheating and happily
included it in the deck after submitting the decklist) will feel
pretty bad about being denied his place in the finals if despite
all odds he manages to gain enough points.

On the other hand... the 6th seed player who played fairly, and
whose decklist is matching, will feel pretty bad about some higher
seed who deliberately changed the contents of his deck to better
cope with the finals (say, by playing 4 Suddens in the prelims,
and writing 2 Sudden, 2 Direct on the decklist to have more
bargaining power in the more diplomatic finals) but who can play
at the finals despite this as the intentionality is not provable,
and the judge uses a "1-2 cards are still only Warning" practice.

Rule #1 of judging - if you need to make a call, that will favor
one person, the other person will feel bad about it.

but fair, egalitarian, and necessary (with the caveats involved: assuming
decklists are requested, assuming the contents of the decks are not
permitted to be changed, etc.).

Referring to the following section of the rulebook:

102. Deck Problem - Illegal Main Deck (Legal Decklist)
Definition:

This penalty applies to tournaments in which decklists are being used.

This penalty applies to players who have misplaced cards from their deck
or have cards from a previous game in their deck.

Players are considered to have an illegal deck when one of the following
conditions is true (while the decklist still indicates a legal deck):

The main deck contains an illegal number of cards.
The main deck contains cards that are illegal for the format.
The contents of the main deck do not match the decklist.
Philosophy:

The decklist is the ultimate guide to a player's deck. If the decklist
indicates a legal deck, but the actual contents of the deck do not match
the decklist, the player should restore the deck to reflect the decklist.
If the judge can determine with complete confidence that the deck/decklist

discrepancy is due to an error on the decklist (a player is using an all
Gangrel deck and has Campground Hunting Ground listed on the decklist
instead of Zoo Hunting Ground), he or she may decide to fix the decklist
instead. A warning should be issued in this case.

Penalty:

Game loss, and then be instructed to make any changes necessary to make
the contents of the deck match what is recorded on the decklist. The
changes must be complete before the next round begins for the player to
continue in the tournament.

...if the judge sees the mismatch between the deck and the
decklist, and he has no *complete confidence* that there is
an error on the decklist (the example is similar to the ones
I gave) then the recommended penalty is the Game Loss.

If the judge suspects actual intentional cheating is involved,
the section on cheating should be consulted, and the penalty
is likely disqualification without a prize (and possible
additional actions by VEKN).

However, as the judge will most likely not take the burden of
judging that the discrepancy is actual cheating (just like he
probably won't have *complete confidence* that it is an error
